A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Long-RVOS and ReferMo. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. All pages were inspected: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes three supplementary pages.

before.justification: Section 5 and Tables 2–3 report original benchmark experiments, SAM2 oracle evaluations and ReferMo ablations.

after.justification: Section 5 and the supplementary material report original benchmark and validation results, component ablations, robustness analyses and dataset statistics.

M1.justification: Both versions use MPEG-4 keyframe/motion decomposition, spatial and channel gating, aligned global object interactions, keyframe supervision and SAM2 propagation. V2 Section 8 supplies additional training and inference specifications; it does not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: The same Long-RVOS dataset, source domains, description-based segmentation task and MeViS oracle comparison remain. Additional validation results and subgroup analyses examine existing coverage. Tasks mentioned in v2's future-work discussion are not evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds RGA3 to the six retained RVOS comparators from v1 Table 2. V2 Table 4c additionally compares XMem++ and Cutie with SAM2 as propagation alternatives. These extend the comparison set without replacing its principal methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the validation/test allocation from 113/225 videos and 1,379/2,588 descriptions to 112/226 videos and 1,326/2,641 descriptions. Training allocation, metrics, resolution and stated training budget remain unchanged. New analyses introduce component controls and grouping by occlusion, description length and keyword-derived event count; these are additional protocols rather than evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands component and robustness analysis: propagation alternatives, global interaction with motion, gating mechanisms, occlusion rates, description lengths, event complexity and qualitative comparisons appear in Tables 4–6 and 10–12 and Figure 8. Tables 7–8 also quantify challenging video attributes. The oracle analysis remains and the keyframe ablation is revised, but v1 Table 3c's motion-length sweep is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional descriptive percentages and result tables do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores change extensively between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. ReferMo's overall J&F/tIoU/vIoU changes from 51.3/71.2/42.6 to 52.9/73.6/45.2, while VideoLISA's overall J&F changes from 33.1 to 14.0. SAM2 oracle and keyframe results also change. V2 adds validation results in Table 9 and numerous analytical results. Because the reported held-out allocation changes, these are revised results, not established same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: V2 Section 8 adds explicit mathematical definitions for motion-vector block matching, the weighted sequence-matching/training cost and inference query selection in Equations 6–8. This is a limited extension of mathematical specification. The metric and fusion mathematics in Equations 1–5 remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a long-term RVOS benchmark, three description types, temporal/spatiotemporal metrics and the motion-enhanced ReferMo baseline. Updating the benchmarked-method count from six to seven expands supporting evaluation without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning MLLM data requirements, motion's role in global reasoning, gating against irrelevant motion, and robustness when keyframes miss objects. Section 12 explicitly discusses task boundaries and excluded background classes. Conversely, v1's caveat about inferior tIoU is replaced by an across-all-types-and-metrics improvement statement, although v2 Table 3 still gives ReferDINO higher hybrid tIoU: 73.1 versus 72.9.

D1.justification: V2 Section 8 substantially expands implementation documentation with block matching, motion-extraction throughput and CPU hardware, cosine-based object matching, training loss components, positive/negative sequence assignment, inference query selection and clip-wise propagation. It also explicitly states that all compared models use no external segmentation datasets. These are newly documented details; the principal hyperparameters, GPU training resources and project-page access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for XMem++, Cutie, RGA3 and Conditional Convolutions for Instance Segmentation, supporting the additional comparisons and implementation description. The related-work categories and central novelty positioning remain stable. ReferDINO's preprint-to-conference citation update represents the same work.

P1.justification: The main six-section narrative remains largely intact, with localized rewriting of the introduction, dataset discussion and experimental interpretations. V2 organizes additional material into supplementary Sections 7–12. This extends the document without extensively rewriting or reordering its existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the predominantly single-column layout with a two-column format and substantially reorganizes displays. Dataset statistics are split across figures, the description-type pie chart becomes Table 2, and v1 Figures 5–6 are merged into v2 Figure 7. V2 also expands the example montage and adds analytical tables and qualitative Figure 8. These changes exceed renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's reproducibility and empirical attribution. Section 8 documents previously unspecified training and inference logic, while propagation, interaction and gating controls help distinguish the contributions of ReferMo's components. Attribute statistics and robustness analyses also substantiate the benchmark's challenges and applicability boundaries. These gains outweigh the removed motion-length sweep and localized reporting problems, including the overstated all-metrics claim and Table 5's inconsistent first-row J&F average. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and diagnostic evidence, not on higher revised scores.
